newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Euro refining margins suffer despite New Year cold.
newsitem.headline: Euro refining margins suffer despite New Year cold.

text.p: European oil refining margins have dropped sharply since December, despite exceptional cold in the first two weeks of the year, leaving refiners desperate for the gasoline market to take off, analysts and oil economists said.
"Typically the first quarter is awful, but after great success at the end of last year, it has come as a bit of a shock," said an economist with a European major.
"Even the best cold weather did not really inspire (margins) in the end," said an economist at a Dutch refinery.
Cold weather at the start of the year resulted in a sharp rise of gas oil prices.

Heating oil barges in Rotterdam, many of which go to the key German market, rose by $13 from year-end to a peak of $238 fob a tonne on January 9. At the time, temperatures in many parts of northwest Europe dropped to below -20 Celsius (-4 Fahrenheit)
"We got a bit of a kick from the cold, but not all that much," said one economist.
The key problem was that gas oil gains were virtually matched by those of crude. Milder weather since then has caused gas oil to slide below $200, while crude has only dipped.
"Basically, crude just held up stronger than the products. Margins were poor even at the beginning of January," said Leslie Owens of oil consultants, Petroleum Economics.
The spread between Brent crude and gas oil (heating oil) futures has fallen $2.88 a barrel to just $4.11 a barrel on nearby contracts since January 10.

Importantly, the swaps market for gas oil crack spreads has also slumped. The second quarter this year now languishes well below $4.00 a barrel having been close to $5.00 towards the end of last year.
Heating oil stocks among wholesalers and end-users have been reasonably high, the result of large-scale buying in late December and in the first week of January. Demand has consequently been slack.

"People just felt fairly comfortable with the stock levels they had accumulated and, with high prices in the cold spell, people just took a risk in not buying any more," said a member of one refinery planning department.
At the refineries themselves, distillate stocks have also risen past year-ago levels as European refiners ran at near maximum capacity.
A steep backwardation, recently engineered by a U.S. trading house, has further discouraged prompt purchases.
In the Mediterranean a lack of arbitrage opportunities to the Asia Pacific region caused deeper gloom.
"In Rotterdam in January, average margins were close to the September/October average, but in the Mediterranean they were very much lower," said Cindy Poynter of oil consultants Bonner and Moore.
Some in the industry have alreay written off the gas oil market.
Refiners are instead already pinning their hopes on gasoline, believing that lower than average stock levels can lift them out of their current trough.

"We're looking for mogas to kick in early. There are signs," one oil economist said. The premium for gasoline above Brent in the critical second quarter has jumped 40 cents a barrel in recent days to $5.40 a barrel.
Refiners' efforts to produce as much distillate as possible late last year meant sacrificing some gasoline output.
"There was an enormous focus on distillates and gasoline stocks were not built up as typically they are," Cindy Poynter.
Poynter said that, at the end of January, she expected gasoline stocks in Europe to be around four percent lower than at the same time last year.
"Of course, there's still an overhang. The export market to the U.S. is vital, but gasoline could end up being at its highest level of the past four years," she said.
Shutdowns due in spring have increased the expectancy, but analysts warn refiners against being overly optimistic about the gasoline market.
Many were similarly bullish at the start of autumn when distillate stocks were low, but peak European production made up all the shortfall.
"The problem is that people are focusing on it (gasoline) already," said Owens.
-- Philip Blenkinsop, Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5004
